utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, I understand there's a matter you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Yes. We filed late last night, about 11.30, a request to delay the motion -- or the testimony of VG-11 based on the late disclosure by the Prosecution. On Sunday evening at 6.40 or so we received additional disclosures in our box of which we picked up yesterday morning but due to of course the court calendar we didn't really get to look at them until yesterday evening. We printed the disclosures, and these are related to VG-11, Your Honour, that is set to -- actually was set to start yesterday, of course, but is starting today. We printed these and there's approximately 200 pages of disclosures all in Serbian, and in there we were able to highlight VG-11's name 60 or so times. One of the issues of which will be relevant for today's testimony, and of course Mr. Rasic wasn't able to really read all of this and translate it and get into the meat and bones of it I would like Mr. Lukic to have an opportunity to read this but one important I think exculpatory issue which is also would be considered a Rule 68 matter is simply that according to this document in one section VG-11 simply spoke to another named witness or someone he'd spoken to and actually put the bus incident or convoy which will be the lion's share of VG-11's testimony on June 17th which would be, you know in comport with our theory of the case. So given the fact I think we do need to go through this a little bit better before we cross-examine VG-11. I know the Prosecution's going to say let's do --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the purposes of interpretation, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Excuse me, a significant amount of preparation involved for this specific witness and considering that this really does go to the heart and bones about what happened around June 14th which of course is the Pioneer Street fire; this is an important witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask the Prosecutor to explain what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honours know that disclosure is constantly ongoing and I issue searches are being conducted on the system-wide searches on witnesses and as documents are discovered they are disclosed. Now, those documents were reviewed, the initially documents were reviewed by me, and the Serbian documents were reviewed by translators, and there was no significant Rule 68 material in that at all and, in fact, I would guess if that's the only incident the witness once said to someone else that it happened on another day. I would venture to say that that is all that might be in those documents. We -- we have a policy of broad disclosure. Those documents are witness statements or reports that were taken over the years that mention this witness's name, just mention his name. Any document that mentions his name is disclosed. It doesn't necessarily mean that it has any significance, any relevance, or any exculpatory information in the documents, and I would suggest that we go ahead with his testimony and the cross that they prepared, and if he has to come back for a limited cross in the future after they've reviewed the documents, then we will bring him back, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say disclosure is an ongoing process, but we do have rules that we apply.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So when was this actually discovered --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- by you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The end of last week when it was disclosed. Document reviews are ongoing on a daily basis. As you know, there are several trials going on. ISU searches are conducted as quickly as the people can do them, and the language assistants are spread thin, and everybody is reviewing documents just as fast as they can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have another witness at hand?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: He's not here. I don't think victim witness is going to bring him here until 11.00, Your Honour. Actually, we have another witness who is scheduled to go after VG-11. He is a 92 bis, and then VG-97 will be testifying. So we have three witnesses lined up for today, but Mr. -- Mr. Spahic has been here for several days and he's prepared to give his testimony, and I think it's only fair to him that he be allowed to come in and give his testimony, and as I said, if they find anything in those documents that they want to ask him about, we can bring him back for limited cross-examination on those -- on those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, this is what the Chamber has decided: The witness will testify as scheduled. However, if there is anything in the documentation that was disclosed very late to you and you wish to cross-examine on it and you are not in a position to do so now, then the witness will be recalled for further cross-examination. The Chamber considers this to be the best way of using the Trial Chamber's time efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, only for the record we were just looking at the disclosure batch on the computer, and the dates of those were last modified either the 6th or the 12th of August. So there was some delay between the disclosure on Sunday on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber has ruled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio, I'd like to say on behalf of the Chamber that while I appreciate that disclosure is an ongoing process, you also must be very careful and do everything in your power to ensure that documentation is disclosed in -- within the time frame set by the Trial Chamber, because if you have matters that are disclosed very late, then obviously the kind of problem which has arisen now will arise, and the Trial Chamber must ensure that its time is used efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I take that to heart. I'll discuss it with the team, and we'll ensure that the documents are disclosed as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Excuse me. That's not the right -- that's the wrong witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a case of mistaken identity. Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I notice that the time that you have allocated for this witness is an hour and a half. That's not so?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think I can conduct my direct within a half an hour as Your Honour instructed for 92 ter witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May begin, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Ferid Spahic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in the spring of 1992 in what municipality or village did you live?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I lived in the village of Smrijece where I was born. That is in Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, sir?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, you testified before this Tribunal in 2001 in the case of Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you recall the dates of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: The 12th and 13th of September, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And, sir, since coming to The Hague a few days ago have you had an opportunity to listen to your testimony in full in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And is everything that you stated in your prior testimony truthful and accurate to the best of your knowledge in regard to the events that you witnessed and experienced in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you the same questions today that were put to you during your testimony in 2001 about these events would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Essentially they would be. Not perhaps word for word, but essentially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In substance they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, in substance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that the testimony be admitted in evidence, 65 ter numbers 70 and 71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And also, Your Honour, there were three exhibits that went to the testimony. I would ask that they also be admitted, or would you like me to ask the witness questions? They were discussed during his testimony, and they're also on our 65 ter exhibit list, so we just asked that they be admitted along with the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: They will be admitted. They are 65 ter number 67, 68, and 69.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, witness statement will become P15; 65 ter 67 will become Exhibit 16; 65 ter 68 will become Exhibit P17; and 65 ter 69 will become Exhibit P18.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Spahic, in addition to giving testimony in the Vasiljevic trial, did you also provide a statement to an ICTY investigator in November of 1997?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I did. I gave that statement in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And the statement was typed in English but read back it you in the Bosnian language at that time, it wasn't?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And since coming to The Hague you've had an opportunity to review your statement in the Bosnian language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And after reviewing your statement did you make certain corrections and addition to this 1997 statement?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I did make certain corrections, and they just involved some slips of the tongue or some minor technical mistakes, typos, but in substance the statement is quite good.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you signed what was called an addendum to your statement which contains these corrections; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you signed the English version of this statement after it was read back to you by a translator in the Bosnian language; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, is everything contained in your 1997, taking into consideration the corrections that you made in the addendum, and is everything in the addendum truthful and accurate to the best of your knowledge in regard to the events that you witnessed and experienced in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is truthful and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you the same questions that were put to you by the investigator in 1997, would your answers be the same as those that you provided and as amended in your addendum?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. In substance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ask that the witness's statement and the addendum be admitted in evidence. We do not have 65 ter numbers for these two statements. However, I have the ERN numbers, ERN 00548587 to 8589. That is the statement. The addendum is 01109684 to 9694. No, sorry. One moment, please. I apologise, Your Honours. Just one moment for the correct numbers. I apologise. The addendum ERN number is 06382599 to 2602.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to make the correction regarding the first witness statement. 65 ter number 70 will become Exhibit P15 and 65 ter number 71 will become Exhibit P19. ERN number 00548587 will become Exhibit P20, and ERN number 063825997 to 2602 will become Exhibit P21.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, as you've heard, your prior testimony and your statement has been admitted in evidence so that the Chamber has the full statement and testimony. So therefore I'm not going to ask you questions and go into any detail about the events that you experienced in June of 1992. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you a couple of questions. Now, your testimony and your statement -- in your testimony and statement you testify about a convoy of buses that was organised in Visegrad to transport people out of the area and presumably to safety; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in your statement and testimony you say that the convoy was supposed to leave Visegrad on the 14th of June. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it did leave Visegrad on the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And on the 14th of June, were you on a bus that was with other buses at the Visegrad Hotel?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was on one of the several buses that were in this column.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And can you tell me how many buses and/or vehicles there were that set out in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I personally did not count the vehicles to establish their actual number, but I do know that there were about five or six buses and two trucks, two lorries with tarpaulins.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And at some point these buses left of the Visegrad Hotel and started out on a route to where?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: They set off on a road that had not been agreed upon. Actually, while we were still there at the square, prior to our very departure, prior to the convoy's very departure, we were offered three routes for the convoy to take. One of them was to Skopje in Macedonia. Another one was to Olovo, and yet a third one was to Kladinja [phoen]. However, the fact is that Skopje was just a decoy to lure us, to get us onto that convoy. In fact, while we were still at the square, in the buses Ljupko Tasic demanded that we make up lists of people on the buses and to indicate the direction which we wanted to take, and I did so in respect of the bus that I was on, and I wrote on the top of that list that the desired direction was Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. But my question to you is at some point on the 14th of June did the buses leave the Visegrad Hotel, and the bus that you were on, in which direction did the bus travel?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: We first went to the bus station in Visegrad for the bus to be refuelled, and then we went back and via the Novi Most, or the New Bridge in Visegrad, we took the direction of Smrijece. That is the byroad, the Visegrad-Rogatica byroad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately what time on the 14th of June your bus left Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure of the exact time, but I think it was between 9.00 and 11.00 that we actually left town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to ask you a question. When you testified in 2001, this was nine years after the events that you lived through in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: How was it that you were able to remember the date of 14 June as the bus leaving -- as the buses leaving Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, I was able to do that because all those dates which are associated with our hapless fate, those dates are etched in my mind. So it is not at all hard for me to recall those dates. I would wish it on no one to experience what I had gone through, so that these dates are eternally etched in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, the actual -- the actual execution that you testified to and is talked about in your statement, is that happened on the 15th of June; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And has the 15th of June had any significance in your life since this event?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it does have. Nothing good is associated with that date except the fact that I'm still alive. Everything else is bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What is your date of -- what is your birthday?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: The 8th of May, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you celebrate a second birthday?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what date is that second birthday?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: The 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And why do you celebrate your birthday on the 15th of June?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: The 15th of June, we were taken to a spot called Paklanik [phoen], that is I, myself and some 50 of my neighbours and friends, family members, with our hands on our backs, and there all these people were executed, and I was the only one who fortunately managed to escape.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So what do you consider the 15th of June to be?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, what can I say? I do not celebrate it as one would celebrate one's birthday, you know, but I do commemorate it in a special way because no 15th of June can pass without my eliciting the scenes of the 15th of June in 1992. It's just impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move on to -- you stated in your testimony that a person walked on the convoy bus before it left Visegrad whom you later learned was Milan Lukic. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you learned the identity of this person?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: At that particular moment we were already ready to depart, the convoy was, when at a certain point this person boarded our bus who I had not seen before, and that person stood just next to my seat. I looked up and then I look at him for three or four seconds, and I again looked in front of me. He just called out the name of Esad Kustura, a schoolmate of his. He actually said schoolmate. I don't know whether they were actually schoolmates, but he said, "Schoolmate, come out." When Esad was passing by my seat I told him to run. However, he reached a last step of the bus while outside there broke out a quarrel between Ljupko Tasic and Milan Lukic. Actually, that man who had been on the bus but at that time I didn't know it was Milan Lukic. After a short talk and a short quarrel, Ljupko said Esad to go back on the bus. Esad, while passing by me said, "Ljupko saved me skin." Later after we had left that spot after we set off in the direction of Orlovo I inquired who that person who boarded the bus was, and Esad told me that it was Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You did not know Milan Lukic before this time, did you?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now I would like to go into the last area of examination and it involves a map, Your Honours. The map is in e-court. However, I have hard copies because I think it's more significant to see, and I prefer that we look at the hard copies if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May I have -- may have just one moment, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir -- can we put it --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can this be shown on the ELMO so the Judges can see where -- thank you. I think that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, could you mark on this map where the town or the municipality of Visegrad is with the -- with the Magic Marker that I gave you.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you circle it.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And put a V by it for Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you recall and if so can you draw the route that the convoy took on the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. The convoy set off from the square in Visegrad. It passed the Novi Most across the Drina River and continued its journey on the asphalt road towards Rogatica by taking the byroad, detour which goes via Smrijece, and the Gornja and Donja Lijeska, and via Gornja and Donja Lijeska, Kopito, Pesurici, up to a place called Seljane which is in the vicinity of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, from that point on, you travelled to another place and then you went back. Can you just tell us briefly from there where you went and where the execution took place?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: We set out from Seljane taking the macadam road through Zakoma and Sakovici [phoen] and we reached the municipality of Sokolac. Then we went on via Knedjina [phoen] to Isarica Brdo and this already is in, I believe, Orlovo municipality. There, unfortunately, and I believe that there was a truck full of soldier who followed this convoy from Sokolac, so at the meadows they just surrounded the convoy so they said the elderly women and children could leave the convoy while all the rest go to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at some point on this route did you spend the night, the evening of the 14th in the buses?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were sent back -- actual -- we were taken back from Isarica Brdo to Sokolac. There we were all crammed in just one bus, and there outside the hotel Romanija the police station in Sokolac we spent the night in the bus with guards watching us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is that place on this map where you spent the evening on the bus?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: No, it is not. No. I would need another map for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Another map going in the same direction as you -- as the convoy was moving? It's off the map?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's on the map. This is just Visegrad-Rogatica direction. I need Rogatica-Sokolac one and a map also showing Orlovo, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, could you point out on this map where Kopito is, and please circle and put a K next to it if you find it.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, is Kopito a town or a village or a place? Could you describe it for us?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I actually couldn't see very well at that particular time, but it passed by that road before, and I was familiar. It is just a few houses scattered by the road so it is not actually a proper village. It is just a couple of houses, perhaps a hamlet, two or three families.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, between Visegrad and Kopito were there any barriers or roadblocks to prevent you from travel on the road?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Not in that section, but later on, somewhere I'm not quite sure, but before Seljani. Possibly at person Rijici, at this spot right here there was some sort of barricade blocking the road. I know we were held there for a couple of minutes. There were some troops there, some soldiers and later after we had passed I saw that it had been only a simple log on the road and who had put it there and why I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But it didn't prevent the convoy from continuing on, did it, this log?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I note that on the map you marked this place where the log was as P; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I suppose that it was at Pesurici, so I put P as the initial of the toponym.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir on the 14th of June of 1992, if you were to drive from Kopito to Visegrad would you take that exact same route that your convoy took?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the only road, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I move that the map be admitted in evidence. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P22, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid. Mr. Alarid, you're up next, as they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I think I'm up next usually, but thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good morning, VG-11.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You indicated in any of your testimonies that you only saw Mr. -- who you understand to be Mr. Milan Lukic one time?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this was related and only happened in the square of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecution spoke to you about your statement of -- I best guess it would be 1997; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And your testimony in Vasiljevic trial; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you also read your statements of September 11th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I looked at the statement, but those were not my words. The substance is the same, and I even believe that the signature on those documents is not mine. And even factually they maiden name of my mother is not Omerovic, it is Drino. Only a short time had elapsed since the events and my statements, so I would ask you if you want to question me to base your questions on my statement that I gave to the investigators from The Hague in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why would you prefer that?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: The statements from 1992 contain the substance, but the substance is too disorderly. Somebody retold my story and it really isn't -- it isn't the right thing. It didn't as it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you also gave a statement 5 December 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Could you give me the place where I gave that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, 1992, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, 1992, I was not in Sarajevo, sir. I was in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd like ERN number 00614799 to 00614808 to be put on, which has been uploaded into e-court as 1D00-0161. That's the B/C/S version. And the English version has been uploaded as 1D00-0152.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Sir, this statement was not made in Sarajevo. It was forwarded to in Sarajevo in some way but I made it at Donji Most in the area of Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you did make a statement 5 December 1992?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I don't remember if it was the 5th of December, but if it's dated December 5 then this probably is true, but it was made at Donji Most, which is close to Visoko. And under what pretense did you give the statement on 5 December?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: For the first time after what had happened to us on the 15th of June I came to the place where the rest of the convoy ended up, the women, children, and the elderly. I'm a man who had survived the execution and who was supposed to tell the truth to those who survived, the wives and children and parents, so that the statement was necessary the way it was. It was given in a haste. It lacks detail, but I had to give it under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true, though, that in neither statement of September 11th 1992, or December 5th, 1992, do you mention Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: That is possible. As soon as I noticed the first mistakes in the statement I didn't continue reading. Those were not my true words. My true words were those that I -- from the statement in 1997. This statement I only gave to satisfy those that were present then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What did you think was necessary to satisfy those who were present investigating this case in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. When I think back to that interrogation in Mostar, I remembered the mistakes the investigators made at the time and that didn't matter to me immediately. I think he retold my words to a lady who made a -- who made the protocol, who put it down on paper. It didn't matter to me. I had lived through the war and all these ordeals. It was essential, it was important that I make a statement and that I give a rough account without thorough analysis. But in 1997, for two days, I testified in Sarajevo, and everything I remembered at the time was put on paper. So if you want to ask me about the statement I made in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: To be honest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness. Witness, you say that you remembered the mistakes the investigators made. What -- what were those mistakes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot point out any mistakes precisely, but when I said a sentence the investigator would either adapt it or rephrase it. It didn't matter to me at the time. As soon as I saw the statement that Djordje Gacic had called the Uzice Corps, which is nonsense. A simple peasant cannot possibly call in an army corps. But as I said, in 1992 I didn't pay attention to those things back in 1992. I had only given -- been given a few days of leave to visit my father so that the statement was given while the impressions of the execution were still fresh. Only a few months had elapsed. So extracting things from that statement I don't think would be a fair thing to do, although in -- in substance it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why didn't it matter to you at the time that mistakes were made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The war was only yet starting. I was given five days of leave to visit my father, and I gave that statement in a haste because I had to go back to the front line. I didn't mind those things at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about the substance of the 1992 statements and then we can talk about how you recalled different things later. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: [In English] No. No. [Interpretation] I only know a few words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, you answered Ms. Sartorio with a yes, and so I assumed you might have. When you were first told --

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: -- that you were going to be given the option of a convoy, some of the people saw this as a salvation; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: That's what we all thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's because you had been hiding from persecution in the woods; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you had also been scouting with binoculars and witnessed other atrocities; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so -- but there was great suffering on the people that were hiding. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- but during that time you -- how long have you been from the Visegrad area?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You were born in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: In the surroundings of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the Visegrad area is -- is not a large area in terms of population?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's why you were able to recognise many names as neighbours and friends, either Muslims or Serbs, during your earlier statements; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say that in your mind, going back to the 15th of June as you say it, the convoy to execute the people on your bus, would you consider that a war crime?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And during that time you gave statements probably hoping that the people responsible for that convoy and executions would be found justice.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Those statements I gave at the time to satisfy the form and in the hope that if I as the only survivor would be killed subsequently, that a written trace would -- would remain behind. But if -- I didn't expect it to take on such a wrong shape. That's why I was glad when I got the opportunity to give another statement, which was 100 per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you were glad because the people that executed your friends were brought to justice?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the people who conducted the execution are still at large, the organiser of the convoy is still at large. And if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Please go on. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Who do you consider the organiser of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: The main organiser of the convoy is Ljupko Tasic, my neighbour from Bosanska Jagodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is it fair to say you consider him responsible for the 50 deaths of the people on that bus?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: If I may, I'll take the opportunity to ask Mr. Milan Lukic. Their conversation in the square in front of bus took a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just stop. You're not to ask any questions here. You answer questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, but the key to the solution lies there. If you wish, we can solve the case of the convoy that was formed on the 14th of June, 1992. Then we -- somebody will have to put that question to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Prosecutor will do that if she considers it appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. VG-11, let me ask you about Mr. Gacic. Do you consider him partly responsible for this convoy?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: We were taken to the convoy because it was suggested to us by our neighbours. Mr. Gacic approached us in the village of Zagre. I trusted him, and he -- he was actually the first bait that we swallowed and got caught.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in terms of the bait do you think that he knew that it was not a convoy to remove you from the area and save you but in fact a convoy to take you to be executed?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I'm convinced that he knew that our convoy was not a convoy of salvation, and those that had organised it had already judged us. They only used the good neighbourly relations that we had before to deceive the people to get on the convoy, and unfortunately that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What about the other local Serbs that you remembered their names, Dusan Maric?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Those people today, as far as I know from some people who returned to Visegrad, live normally. I must also say that Ljupko Tasic, upon the questions of some returnees what had happened to the people on the convoy, answered that he is not to blame for anything and that the decision to execute us was taken by Milan Lukic in the square when he turned up, and that's why it is important for me to know what the conversation was that they had in the square. It was very brief, only a few sentences, and I believe that conversation relieves Milan Lukic of the responsibility of that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You believe that conversation relieves him of responsibility? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Milan Lukic simply appeared and wanted to take his schoolmate out of the bus. I think that during those months there was -- there wasn't probably anybody who could prevent Milan Lukic from doing something that he wanted to do, but Ljupko Tasic at that moment prevented him from taking Esad off the bus, and that -- it was impossible to achieve unless Milan Lukic promised to Ljupko Tasic something -- or, rather, the other way round.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, who is Ljupko Tasic and what was his profession?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: He was a neighbour of mine. I must say that we were on good terms. He was a haulier. He had some machines, some baggers. We've known each other since birth. We never had any problems with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But he had no problem taking you to be executed.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it's easy to assume that all the people that either escorted you to the place of the execution all knew the fate of you and the fate of your brothers?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: All the events around the execution were experienced through something of a haze, a haze of disbelief. I can only say that the guys who actually executed those people knew very well how to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What about Rade and Sladjan Simic?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: They were also neighbours of mine. Rade owned a pub at Bosanska Jagodina. We had a meeting there on the 13th of June with Ljupko Tasic. I wanted to find out what kind of convoy that was, because sometime ago a similar convoy had been organised by Milan Lukic, and 17 or 19 people ended up in the vicinity of Bosanska Jagodina. I'm not an eyewitness. I only heard accounts from other people and from the families of those that were executed, and among those 17 or 19 people there was also a relative of my wife. He is the only one who was buried at the cemetery, and the remains of the others were found in a chasm some eight kilometers from Visegrad, but only about half of the bodies. I only went to Bosanska Jagodina to prevent the same thing from happening to us too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But yet in your statement of 5 December 1992 when you mentioned the fate of the 17 people on the earlier convoy, you made no mention of Milan Lukic being responsible.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: When did I make that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, you simply made the statement that you wanted to make sure that the same fate didn't happen to your convoy that happened to the 17; but you did not indicate Milan Lukic's name, nor that you believed that he was responsible. And I believe that's on page 2 of the statement in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: That is possible. At the moment I possibly didn't know that Milan Lukic was responsible for that convoy. I still do not know, but based on the accounts of other people whose family members ended up there, it must have been Milan Lukic. But there were bodies found there and DNA analyses were conducted, and the remains found were buried. And it is beyond doubt that an execution was conducted. But based on the conversations I had and from people who know Milan Lukic, at the all say that it is his responsibility. I knew about this event, and I went to Bosanska Jagodina to talk to our neighbours to avoid the same thing from happening -- that the same thing happens again. And about this convoy of 17 or 19 people, I cannot say much because I'm not competent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, you have used 25 minutes. I'll give you another 20 unless you really need more time. Generally I'll allow 45 minutes, but you may request additional time, and if I consider it justified then I'll give it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But yet in your third statement of the 3rd and 4th of November, 1997, you again did not mention Milan Lukic in relation to the convoy of 17 people. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the only thing that you mentioned was that Milan Lukic asked for Zenga to get off the bus in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so would it be fair to say that it's possible that Mr. Lukic was trying to take Zenga off the bus because he was a friend and maybe he knew where you might be going, what your fate might be?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I don't know. It is possible that he wanted just to take him for a drink. I mean, that is really nonsense. That is impossible. Zenga was just to be taken off the bus at that moment and be liquidated. That is a fact, because that was the only thing that was going on in Visegrad was killing. Killing was the order of the day. People didn't eat. People didn't drink. The fact that they were schoolmates really change anything, didn't make any difference. And as for this conversation between Ljupko and Mr. Milan it just resulted in Esad getting back on the bus. What this famous sentence was what the substance of that dialogue was whereby Esad managed to get back on the bus that is something that Milan knows and I also know. I know this particular sentence. I've known it for the last 16 years but it is really too no avail because I'm the only one who does know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you're convinced Tasic knew your fate from the meeting on the 13th. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Please, these are assumptions. I suppose so. Actually, I'm quite clear that it was so. I'm quite sure that it was so. But I should like to say once again that Ljupko Tasic simply, when talking to the returnees claim that Milan Lukic had changed the overall concept of the convoy in the square.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I didn't know if you were going to ask a question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. No. You go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So is it possible that Mr. Tasic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is it possible that Mr. Tasic is simply passing the blame to Mr. Lukic so he can live at peace in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object at this point. I don't know what he can get into the mind of Mr. Tasic at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. Ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. Tasic assumed -- appeared to have command responsibility of this convoy, did he not?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was actually with him that I made this deal, and we made the arrangements. In fact, the meeting at the pub could not start without him. We waited for him for some 20 minutes, meaning that after all he was the person in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he also told the other escorts and drivers what to do?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: They moved the buses at his direction?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was Mr. Milan Lukic or who you believe to be Milan Lukic wearing when he tried to get your friend off the bus?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: If you are referring to the three or four seconds -- that three or four seconds that I had available to me, afraid as I was to actually take in the details that is really impossible. I just looked at his face and then I bent my head again. At that time one didn't just actually look at Milan Lukic. It wasn't a done thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You didn't know who Milan Lukic was at the time. Why would it matter?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: The man simply stood by my seat, and instinctively I looked up and I looked at his face, and then I gazed down again. This was done instinctively on my part. If he gone to the seat behind me I wouldn't have known it was Milan Lukic. I would have known from other people telling me that but I wouldn't have seen him myself up to today, and today however is the second time that I see him. The first time that I saw him he really was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you can tell me that you can recognise a man who has aged 16 years after seeing him for three seconds and not knowing his name and not knowing who he was until afterwards, not mentioning his name until 1997?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I just have to clarify something for you. Those moments when someone is actually deciding your fate, life or death, your mind in such moments it registers everything. In hindsight, looking back at all these years, in the reports that I saw in the media, I saw Milan Lukic many times in the media reports, on television and so on. So this is not actually the second time that I see him. This is the second time that I see him in person, in the flesh. And believe you me, it is possible to take in one's face within the space of two or three seconds and have it etched in one's mind forever. It is possible, but one has to experience it. One has to experience some terrible ordeal in order for one's mind to react in that way. I believe if we had a drink then I wouldn't have remembered his.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But do you think someone with all the responsibility and command power would be able to snap his fingers and have Mr. Kustura off the bus, no problem?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: That is the key, in fact. If you want us to unlock this lock, please tell the -- relate to Their Honours just the dialogue that Milan Lukic had conducted with Ljupko Tasic. It is just a couple of sentences. Of course if Milan Lukic remembers that dialogue, then I think he should remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say if Mr. Lukic had no power to tell Mr. Tasic one way or another what to do he is not the Milan Lukic that the media has made him out to be, the stories? You would have expected more?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. I know what you're aim at -- aiming at. I've already said Milan Lukic could not be opposed by anybody. No one could stand up to Milan Lukic in those days. What it was that Ljupko Tasic promised to Milan Lukic at that particular moment outside the bus which made Milan Lukic sway in the other direction and leave the convoy, I don't know that. What --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: -- it was. It's impossible. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Who had power --

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: That's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Who had power in Visegrad at that time? Who had the SDS put into power in Visegrad at that time?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know whom the SDS had appointed to be in power. I believe it was Savovic, but I don't think it matters. I think that all the power was in the hands of paramilitary units. Milan Lukic and the others who were there, some White Eagles and what have you, that's where the power was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please not overlap with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about him also. I think it's Professor Perisic. If that's whom you mean, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he also was chief and commander of the police?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, it was degenerates of that kind that they usually appointed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What do you mean by degenerates?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: That man was not a man for that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: He was the commander, the komandir of the police in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Witness, you've been talking about the dialogue between Milan Lukic and Tasic on the bus as being the key to unlock the -- the puzzle. You heard this dialogue, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why do you believe it will be the key to unlock the puzzle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It indeed is the key to this riddle because no one could oppose Milan Lukic in those days in Visegrad. Why did he listen to Ljupko Tasic and not to take Esad Kustura off the bus if he had that power and he did? What was it that Ljupko Tasic promised to Milan Lukic? That is it. Actually, he didn't promise him anything. It's just that Ljupko Tasic knew what fate would befall us. It's just that he conveyed to him what he already knew. So if Mr. Milan Lukic remembers, recalls that sentence, let him publicly utter it here because I know that sentence. I've known it for the last 16 years, but it is to no avail in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How have you known it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What do you believe that sentence to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I asked how did you know this sentence? How did you get to know this sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For 16 years now I've been living with this crime. I've been putting to the mosaic and the tiles, arranging the tiles. Someone here is responsible for that. Someone has promised me, including the Red Cross, the direction to Skopje and that I would be escorted by my neighbours, Serbs. I was promised this. Nothing was actually honoured, but things took a quite different turn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I want to find out, because you are here to -- to give evidence, to assist the Trial Chamber in determining the facts in this case, and if you say you have known this sentence for 16 years, the Trial Chamber is interested in finding out what it is that you know and how you obtained that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you that sentence, but I just wanted to have it confirmed. In order to save someone at that moment Milan Lukic had to be promised something. At that moment, Ljupko just told Milan not to make a fuss there in the square, that we had already been designated for execution. That was satisfactory for Milan Lukic and for him to leave the convoy. That was enough for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And how -- how do you know that Milan was told this by Ljupko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, everything that was unfolding surrounding this convoy. It had all been deliberate. It had all been planned. On the morrow, on the 15th of June, we ended up at the pit. Had we actually passed, gone on with that convoy, these conversations would all be irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that you have deduced this from all the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll take the break now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, you have four minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I do believe the team of Sredoje Lukic was going to offer some of their time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I believe that the Sredoje Lukic team was going to allocate some of their time as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mean allocate some of their time to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave we have just a couple questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Right. So how much longer do you intend to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, there's three statements, Judge, and there are some more inconsistencies to go into. I would as a practical matter like to introduce the 11 September 1992 statements and the 5 December 1992 statement into evidence. The 11 September 1992 1D00-0145, and the December 5th statement, 1992, is 1D00-0152.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you want to have those admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, they're admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 1D00-0145 will become Exhibit 1D6 and 1D00-0152 will become Exhibit 1D7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. 11, let's talk about the other people that participated in the execution at the end of your trip that day. Do you recall the day of the week?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: It was the 15th of June. I don't know the day of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I mean did you have any other activities that would tell you whether it was a weekday or a weekend?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell me the people that participated in the execution, either by escorting, driving, or shooting.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I only know two people, Predrag Milisavljevic, who started the execution, and Boris Ceho, who was standing -- who was standing on the side close to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Boris Ceho was a reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: It is true, and at the time he was wearing the uniform of a reserve police officer. I also used to be a reserve police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How many other people in that detail were wearing uniforms of policemen or reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I think that only Boris Ceho was wearing such a uniform of a reserve police officer. And apart from these two there were another nine people there, a total of 11 as far as I could tell at the moment and as far as I remember. Eleven people were at the pit. I know that the guy who when Predrag Milisavljevic started the execution at the pit had a flak jacket on him. He was wearing a flak jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Over his uniform?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Predrag clearly told other people what to do?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: That's an interesting thing that nobody commanded anybody there. They gave the impression of a well-trained team who knew what they were doing. I never heard a single command being said. But it's a fact that Slavisa Vukojicic who, didn't know at the time, he's from Rogatica, only after my escape did other people tell me his name based on my description. He seemed to be in charge, and I believe that he was wearing no arms, no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that as of your December 1992 statement you had learned that Baja Zukic had been killed?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: The name must be wrong. Zukic. Yes, that's the last name, but it is not Baja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. What is her first name?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: We're talking about a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: There were no women at the pit. There were men exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you misunderstand me. I'm talking about after your escape you later learned that Ms. Zukic had been killed somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I heard that the following convoy that left after ours -- on the other convoy there was a woman who was killed. It's possible that it was Ms. Zukic, but I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you never heard the name of Milan Lukic associated with Ms. Zukic?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Behija Zukic, whether she was really killed on one of those convoys or in town, in her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you don't know.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: If are talking about the person I mean Behija Zukic, she was killed in her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you did not hear Milan Lukic associated with this?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I did, that Milan Lukic was mentioned in connection with the killing of Behija Zukic if we're talking about the same person, I mean the one who had a house in Duce.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you didn't mention Mr. Lukic in your December 1992 statement, so you later learned of this between 1992 and 1997?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I think I knew that even before that time, but the statement I gave in two, I've already described the circumstances in which it was given. I was still under the impression of my or deal, because this isn't anything I know first-hand. I only heard accounts from other people. I didn't see it. I don't know for sure. I heard lots of things. We can talk for days about all the things I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, would it be fair to say all the things you heard about Milan Lukic was sometime between your December statement of 1992 and 1997 because you never mention him till 1997?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I really cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, you didn't know who Milan Lukic was in the square at Visegrad when you were on the bus; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the only word you got was that a name was mentioned that day that you didn't remember until 1997; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: No. I heard that name on the very same day on the bus. I asked Mirsad Zukic, who the man was who got on the bus, and he told me. I don't know if they were schoolmates, but Milan Lukic called Esad out by calling him a schoolmate. So I knew that it was Milan Lukic on that very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you knew on that very day that he did not have the power to take him off the bus?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: On the following day I found out that Milan Lukic did have a lot of power, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You found that out on the following day but never mentioned it even in 1997?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, probably nobody ever asked me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you didn't mention it in your testimony of 2001?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, probably even then nobody asked me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But would it be fair to say that based on your overall understanding of the power structure in Visegrad, the Crisis Staff and Perisic had the control in town?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Dear sir, if I may ask you one thing. Is there one single protocol about the crimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute, please. You are not to ask questions. That is counsel's right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As far as I know, there is no single protocol about the crimes committed at the police station mentions Perisic, but certain crimes were committed, and this is a clear evidence that the police was not what they were supposed to be, that they were all involved in crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And they were led by Perisic?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Perisic was my teacher, unfortunately. Who he led and where I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you testified in the trial of Mr. Vasiljevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in that trial you testified that you didn't learn that Milan Lukic -- his name until later; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But nothing about that conversation told you that he was in power; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Which conversation do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The conversation where you learned his name for the first time.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the entire question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That there was nothing about the conversation where you learned Milan Lukic's name that told you he had any position of power or responsibility.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I heard about Milan Lukic from the very beginning of the war actions in Visegrad but that's all. I only heard about him, and until the end of the war I heard stories about his actions, but these are things I cannot comment upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true in your testimony before the Tribunal you indicated that you were confused why only Mitar Vasiljevic was charged with these crimes of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I may have said that if that's what the transcript says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You knew Mitar Vasiljevic had -- had drinks with him casually?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was all before the war started. We were even on good terms. We had more drinks than just a few together with Mitar -- or, rather, fortunately I never met Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Unfortunately?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately. Actually, I said fortunately. I said fortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You never met him after the war started is what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But nothing about his -- his demeanour told you that he would be a monster during the war. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, look here. Visegrad is a very small town. It is a beautiful town, at least it used to be up to the war, where everybody knew everybody. It is inconceivable, for instance, for a -- for schoolmates to kill one another. It was inconceivable. And the same thing applied to Milan. As for Mitar Vasiljevic, and actually in respect of everybody who is proved who have been or even not proved to have been something of the kind, well, I've lived through too many things in order not to remember the situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But would it be fair to say that a guy like Mitar Vasiljevic couldn't have killed the thousands that died or disappeared in the Visegrad area during that time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the question. I mean, first of all it calls for speculation. I don't know if this witness -- there has been no foundation laid whether this witness would know that answer, and it really, quite frankly, isn't relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. You must move on and focus your cross-examination, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a proffer to the Court in terms of relevance, one, I believe that the witness has been allowed to speak from points of speculation at many junctures in this testimony, both on direct exam by the Prosecution and well as just his general knowledge of the area. I think his overall knowledge of Milan Lukic is based on speculation and rumours and stories that transcended years of this conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Move on. I'm not allowing the question. Ask another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that in the area, as far as you know, thousands of people were displaced or killed?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And many Muslim mosques and homes were burnt and destroyed?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this took the coordinated effort of hundreds, if not more, Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And prior to this -- or at the time that you were going through this you had never heard the name of Milan Lukic in a position of power. You only heard stories later.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I had heard these stories about Milan Lukic even prior to joining the convoy, but I was not at all interested in that person. I didn't even know who that man was. It was totally immaterial to me. It was unimportant who he was or what he did. Simply what I knew from these stories was that his chief occupation during these months in 1992 was killing. Nothing good. Nothing, absolutely nothing good. From all the things that I heard about -- in all the things that I heard about Milan Lukic there was nothing good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you realise that today is the first day that you've ever said that you heard about Milan Lukic before the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I object to the question. He can say the first time he's ever said in the three statements that are before him, but we don't know what he's said to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question that counsel put was that today is the first time that he never said he heard about Milan Lukic before the 14th of June, and what is -- what's wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, said to whom is what's wrong with that. First time he's ever said -- I think counsel should rephrase the question that -- with relation to the statements that are the subject of this examination, not whether he's ever made a statement to anybody ever in the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, put it in context. Are you talking about the first time that he said in relation to the statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But more generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm actually saying it in relation to the statements and his prior testimony in Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So, Mr. 11, I'll re-put the question to you. Isn't it true that under oath this is the first time that you've mentioned Milan Lukic or knowledge of him before the 14th of June? This is the first time in court today, yet you've had four, five opportunities with authorities to say it before?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: This is the first time that we are dealing with the subject of Milan Lukic. This is the first time that I am talking the witness stand in the case against Milan Lukic. So it is quite possible that we might ferret out some other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: On the -- in December -- excuse me. How long was your interview in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: It was given in Mostre; right? The conversation, rather, the statement that I gave to investigators in Mostre, if that is what you're referring to, lasted from 1400 hours in the afternoon until 10.00 p.m., until 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so during all those hours reliving what had happened to you in those three days and those responsible in the Visegrad area you failed to mention the name of Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, I repeat. I gave that statement just to satisfy the procedural requirements. I did not actually pay any attention to details. It is so full of shortcomings that statement. It is incomplete. As I said before, the war had only just started. I was given some time off to visit my father and to go back, so I lost a day of statement-giving time. Had I known that I would survive the war and I would be sitting here today, certainly this statement from 1997 would have replaced the one from 1992. The way things stand, unfortunately that's the way it had to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So let's jump forward to the statement of 1997. You gave a statement that was translated into nine pages in English; correct? And you signed and initialed those pages?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it was otherwise ten pages in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I do not remember the exact number of pages, believe me, but I do know that I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in that statement you only mentioned Milan Lukic in relation to just finding out his name and no background knowledge about him with any specificity or no leadership responsibility information?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: This has been extracted from context, I guess. If that is what it says, that's the way it was. I do not have that entire statement in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in fact, you only saw White Eagles there but you only heard he was a member of the White Eagles is what you said in your statement of December -- excuse me, of November 1997.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is true that that is what I said in 1997, but after having re-read this statement, I actually saw that that was superfluous, because the White Eagles didn't have white wings for one to be able to see that they were indeed White Eagles. I found it superfluous to comment on that. I just heard that Milan Lukic was a member of the White Eagles. Now, if that is relevant, namely what I heard, well, that is actually why I corrected my statement subsequently and actually took out these two sentences from that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But what you did say in at that statement was specifically that Ljupko Tasic told Milan Lukic that Esad couldn't leave the bus.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: In this context, the way you put it or the way it was translated to me, well, in respect of that it is the fact that Esad told me in passing, "Ljupko has saved me," or, "Ljupko put me back on the bus." That was my statement. And that Ljupko told Esad to get back on the bus, I didn't hear that, and I do not stand by that, and I cannot say that that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the first time you ever said that that Zenga said that Ljupko saved me was today in court.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: It is possible. Perhaps I said it in a different context. It is very difficult to repeat verbatim words that were uttered seven or nine years ago, but the substance I expect is the same. You don't expect me to know these sentences or statements by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But in fact the irony is that Zenga was wrong and Ljupko had in fact killed him?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: No. Ljupko killed no one. Ljupko had prepared the groundwork, everything for the murder to come about.
