So this saving of him, this deliverance in the square was just a travesty in order to avoid any fuss and to avoid any protests among the people, but everything had been agreed on beforehand and actually events bore that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you never got any information that Mr. Lukic participated in this collaboration beforehand?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: No. No. I had no such information. From the very few returnees to Visegrad who still unfortunately have dealings or communication with Ljupko Tasic I heard this, and he is saying that he is not to blame for anything and that that encounter was used in the square in order to shift all the blame to Milan Lukic. This is what I heard. Although I do think if Milan Lukic remembers the conversation in the square that that solves many things. I've already said so before, and I have said what happened at that very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And if Milan Lukic told you that he tried to save Zepa and had no power to do so, would you believe him?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Oh, come on. That's ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tasic refused his request.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Milan Lukic knows that best. I've already said. The conversation that was conducted outside partially or entirely exonerates Milan Lukic of responsibility for this convoy. If Milan Lukic knows what that conversation was about I would ask for that to be told publicly. If not, then this label sticks, which is also a possibility, namely that Ljupko Tasic is now shifting the responsibility onto the shoulders of Milan Lukic, and that of course is possible too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you just don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Would you -- you would have to repeat the question so that I could see what it is that I don't know that you're referring to as me not knowing it, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You don't know if Ljupko Tasic is simply shifting the blame onto Milan Lukic because he's charged here in court.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the story now from Ljupko's mouth, but I repeat I heard it all. I didn't see it, nor did I talk to Ljupko myself. But it is a fact that according to Ljupko's words, Milan Lukic actually had this civilised and normal, regular convoy transformed into one of death. Not in these very words, I have dramatised it a bit, but when all is said and done that's what it amounted to. The only thing which I did see which is relevant is the conversation that they had in the square, and it is a fact that after that conversation Milan Lukic left the convoy and I never saw him again in my life. Therefore, that conversation of theirs was satisfactory. It was enough for Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you realise that Milan Lukic is not accused of the murder of the people on your convoy?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, I confirm that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When did you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: For the murder of people -- not -- not the killing of people. Milan Lukic was not at the pit when these people were executed at the pit on the 15th of June. I claim that with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But do you realise that he's not accused of any responsibility in the planning or execution of a plan to murder the people on the bus with you that day?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: It is possible that he is not charged with that, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is it possible he's not responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: I just say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, it appears to me that you have spent enough time on this issue. He's not charged with it. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you feel that the 111 or so people that ended up at the pit that day should have been charged?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: These were people who were merely discharging the dishonourable task of killing people. Of course for the crime of murder they should be put on trial, as well as should be the masterminds of this entire operation. It is not just 11 people who simply took some weapons, picked up some people and killed them off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That question escaped me. I don't see its relevance. If you do not have any other relevant questions you should stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, the relevance goes to bias or motive to fabricate and or place the blame on someone since so few people were actually charged with the Visegrad crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be heard for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I think my colleague for the Defence has pointed out the accused are not charged with this crime. There's -- this witness is not here to testify that the accused participated in this crime, and I think this has gone on -- this doesn't have anything to do with this witness's credibility in terms of what actually happened to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It has some relevance and I've allowed the cross-examination to follow that course, but you must move to another topic now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour, to check my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know where the White Eagles were supposedly garrisoned?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you have any information on -- and there --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, my case manager indicates there was an issue on translation, maybe with regard to "garrisoned."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know where the White Eagles were staying in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: It doesn't make any difference. The answer is the same. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And even at most all you had heard was that Milan Lukic was supposedly a member of these White Eagles but not a leader?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I don't remember now. What I do know is from the statements of many people, and that is that his was the last word. Now, whether he was the actual leader or not, that is less important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You saw no insignia or special uniform that day?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Not -- nothing specific that would actually stick in my mind. On that day I had different problems. I had problems in my own mind when I saw that on -- at that time on the 14th of June. It was the end of liberty. We had no more rights. We were disenfranchised. These are problems of a quite different ilk than whether someone was wearing a cockade or this or that or insignia. That didn't seem important at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But in fact you didn't see a symbol or a cockade?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: It is totally unimportant. Even had I seen one all the events that ensued afterwards would have deleted that from my memory. The -- that's how immaterial it was. But definitely now I don't think -- I didn't see a cockade. There were different badges but I didn't see one of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, you must bring your cross-examination to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I have three more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There will be no time left for your colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir. One other question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Of the gentlemen that did commit the excuses at the pit, how many were blonde?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: As for the descriptions of all these people, I believe that they are perhaps in one of these statements. Slavisa Vukojicic was blonde and as I recall he was the only markedly blonde person there. How relevant that is now I really don't know. I didn't look to see who was blonde or not. At that moment everybody could have been blonde. But to answer your question precisely, Slavisa Vukojicic was definitely blonde and I believe the others were not. And one of them was grey haired.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did the blonde gentleman have any tattoos on his arms?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: He was wearing a T-shirt with folded up -- rolled up sleeves. So I actually didn't notice, and it didn't even occur to me to look and see whether he had a tattoo or not. He could have had or been anything at that particular moment in time, but it really didn't catch my perception or observation. In fact, that man had beat me up at Rogatica, but I didn't know whether he had a tattoo or not, which didn't mean that he did not have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: My name is Jens Dieckmann. I am co-counsel for Mr. Sredoje Lukic and I have just a very few questions for you. You know Sredoje Lukic; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: If you can say that two encounters in one's life make one person know another person than we do know each other. We had a very brief encounter, the first one in the square. This is our second one, and that's the extent to which I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm speaking about Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. I apologise. I do know Sredoje Lukic well. He was a policeman before the war in Visegrad, and my brother was the deputy komandir at that police station. He was working in the transport section. I was at the petrol station and those went one together, so we had quite a few drinks together, and unfortunately it is a pity that we are not having them today as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And you know Sredoje Lukic as a family man being married with two children at this time, small children?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: No. No. I know Sredoje Lukic just as himself, Sredoje Lukic. He never took out any of his family members of his to have drinks with me, so I just know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: From your personal experience with Sredoje Lukic, do you agree with me that Sredoje Lukic is a friendly person, a good person of a good character?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: To the extent that can or cannot be of assistance in this case. All these people who have been proved or to have committed crimes or those whose crimes will be proven --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute. Witness, you're asked whether from your personal experience with Sredoje Lukic whether you would agree that he's a friendly person, a good person of good character. Now, that question is a question that in my view you can answer. What is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I know it's a little out of order --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I hit the button but it didn't go. Your Honour, just based on one follow-up -- and literally one follow-up question based on the cross-examination of Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. 11, would it be fair to say that what you know of Mr. Sredoje Lukic and what little you know of Milan Lukic that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It is not raised from direct examination and my learned friend Mr. Alarid had the opportunity to ask those questions from his examination. So this is something which is raised from our cross-examination and pursuant to my opinion it is allowed to ask right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why is that? You haven't heard the question. You're saying any questioning by Mr. Alarid now is out of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But with your leave my client is not mentioned during his examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I agree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And any mention of my client immediately is my reaction in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I understand Mr. Cepic wants to protect his client and to be honest the point I'm trying to make doesn't hurt his client. It's merely a point I'm trying to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. 11, this again goes back to your personal knowledge of Sredoje Lukic, and I understand you know very little about Milan Lukic. Would it be fair to say that given Sredoje Lukic's age and position in the community at the time that he wouldn't have been in a position to have taken orders from a man like Milan Lukic, a younger man?

utterances.speaker: FERID SPAHIC
utterances.text: Those were different times. I don't know their hierarchy. Those were different times, times of war. What kind of hierarchy was in place among them? Who gave out orders, who received orders, that has to do with their structure. I cannot give you any information pertaining to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But, sir, that's not the question I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That's enough. I am not going to have that pursued. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just sum up in two or three sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not for you to sum up, Witness. I appreciate your -- the interest you have taken in the case, but your function has come to an end. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls VG-047 to the stand, and my colleague Rachel Friedman will be handling the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin, Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: My name is Mevsud Poljo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Poljo, where were you living in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: In June of 1992, I lived in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And what was the name of the town?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I'm not sure that Zepa was a municipality at the time. I believe the -- it belonged to the municipality of Rogatica. I lived in a village.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And the name of the village, please?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: The name of the village. Slap, it is Slap. I lived in a house in Slap, which was in the outskirts of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Poljo, do you recall testifying here in the Vasiljevic trial on December 17 and 18th, 2001?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Since coming to The Hague are you had a chance to listen to that testimony in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Was the testimony accurate?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: If we asked you today the same questions that you were asked then, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution moves to tender into evidence 65 ter numbers 113 and 114, which was the evidence that was given in the Vasiljevic trial by Mr. Poljo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 113 will become Exhibit P23 and 65 ter number 114 will become Exhibit P24.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: The Prosecution also movers to tender into evidence 65 ter number 112, and that is the aerial photograph of Slap that the witness referred to during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P25, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I may ask just a few questions to supplement that testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Poljo, when you and a group of men pulled bodies out of the river in June and July 1992, can you tell me how many bodies you were able to retrieve?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: 170 or 180-odd corpses.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And of those how many did you personally recognise?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Close to 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did you know where those victims had come from?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: The bodies were washed up in the Drina River from the direction of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And was there anything on the bodies that made you think that they had come from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: They were people who had lived in Visegrad, who worked in companies in Visegrad, and some of my neighbours who lived nearby in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Which companies did some of those people work in?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Terpentin and Varda, Visegrad. They had uniforms and in their pockets they also had coupons on which there was the name of -- there were the names of those firms.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: One final matter, Your Honours the aerial photograph of Slap was discussed in prior testimony but it was not marked. Would that assist you if we were to call that up now and make a few markings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Will the court usher please call up Prosecution Exhibit 25. Thank you. And can it be rotated? Yes. Perfect. Thank you. Yes. And could the court usher assist the witness with the marking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure I understand what I'm supposed to mark.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We haven't begun yet. I will certainly explain that to you. Thank you, Mr. Poljo. Okay. First will you please mark your own initials and today's date, the 26th of August, on the bottom of the photograph. You can use it as if it were a real pen.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please take the pen and mark an arrow on the body of water in the direction the water flowed. Sorry, should say in the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can you just confirm for me the name of the river that you have marked now?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: It was called Zepa, just as the place, the nearby place is called Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So can you identify the Drina River? Mark a D on the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And which way on that river did the water flow? Can you mark an arrow please?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you just write the letter V in the general direction of Visegrad town.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And lastly, if you could please write an X at the location where you buried the bodies. The approximate location. I know it's a rather large stretch.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to now tender this marked photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P26, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. 47, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, approximately how long did you take it upon yourself to recover bodies from the Drina?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: We recovered one body in mid-May and the others in June and July and some in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And from your -- did you do it in a boat or did you do it from the shore?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I recovered some bodies when I was in a boat. I recovered some bodies from the Drina, and for a week the bodies were floating on the river. Nobody recovered them. And then as I had a brother who worked at Terpentin, actually two brothers and an uncle and others, and then we decided to recover bodies to at least make it possible to know where their graves were. And then later on two others joined me in recovering bodies using boats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, of course you can't tell -- just because you recovered a body you can't necessarily tell who killed them?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: No. I don't know that. That's -- it happened far away, over 20 kilometres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is -- so Visegrad, the town, is 20 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Twenty kilometres or possibly more. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because of course you don't know exactly where exactly it was put in the water, do you?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: No. There is no way you can tell, because they were in a bad state. Some were in a better state, some in a worse state. Some were -- probably got stuck on the way and remained in a place for a while. I remember two bodies that had bullet holes. They were from a village nearby, Ibrahim and Hamed Vusevic [phoen] one had two bullet holes, one in the throat, the other in the chest. Those were fresh bodies, clean, and in their pockets they had what people use for personal hygiene, and they had their arms raised to -- as -- as if to defend themselves from the bullets. All the other bodies were in a bad state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that in this case you've had an opportunity to give statements on three separate occasions and then testify at trial on one occasion over two days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clarify he hasn't given three statements in this case. One in relation to the Vasiljevic case, two others long before. I just want to make sure that's clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I understand, and we'll stipulate to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say, Mr. 47, that the only time in the three statements that you mention Mr. Milan Lukic or Mitar Vasiljevic was in the third statement given the 30th of January, 2000?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I don't remember when I mentioned Milan or Mitar given the fact that these things happened 20 kilometres or so away from the place where I was. How could I have a said anything about it? Or perhaps I misunderstood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, actually isn't it true that in your January 30, 2000 statement you simply said, "I also heard rumours that Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic committed a lot of atrocities in the area"?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yeah, well, that's all hearsay, but I'm not a -- I'm not an eyewitness. I never saw anything with my own eyes. I only heard stories from many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you knew Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic before and after this occurred, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I knew Mitar. We were good friends and buddies. His wife worked in the same company where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And accordingly you knew his kum Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I didn't know Milan so well. I knew Sredoje much better. He was a police officer in Visegrad, and I was on good terms with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in fact in your interview with the Prosecution just the other day, you indicated that these accused were part of a greater system, a larger political situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I only know that Sredoje was a police officer before the war and at the very beginning of the war. I don't know about Milan. He wasn't in Visegrad. He worked somewhere in Serbia. I rarely saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he was the younger cousin of Sredoje?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes. I worked near their place of residence in a shop, and I knew Sredoje's parents well. We were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And as part of the rumours, you never heard that Milan Lukic was in a position of authority over anybody?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to say that. I heard lots of stories, but it isn't from my immediate experience. And if I may say about Sredoje, I only heard good things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that Sredoje would not take orders from his younger cousin who was probably 23 years old at the time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Objection. This is speculation. The witness has said that he barely knew either one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in terms of hearing only good things, you never heard that he was given orders by Milan to do anything?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I did hear that he was afraid of Milan, that Milan was in charge of everything, and Sredoje was merely a policeman, and he probably only executed orders, the orders given to him by his superiors. I remember when he took in a neighbour of his, a Muradif Kalic [phoen], a Muslim, and he brought him in at the beginning of the war. He probably wanted advice. I don't know exactly. Took him to Prelovo. That's where the command of the Uzice Corps was. And he took him to a Granap, to Blace, and he took him to the neighbouring village to a guy who was a Vojvoda in the war of 1941 and had done a lot of bad things in the surrounding villages, and he -- that man was taken there to be tested, and he said, "I brought to you this Muslim for you to judge him. You are older than the commander in Prelovo." He possibly would have been convicted and killed, and the -- this name of -- this man by the name of Bozo Ivanovic was then to judge him. And there was another man from Serbia there. So old Bozo then told him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Next question, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so who in fact though was the main power structure in place by the SDS in Visegrad at the time of the war?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I haven't the slightest idea. Around one month before the war I could not go to the town. I was working in one shop, and I passed there two times. There were barricades that would be erected at night. So I just passed through an acacia tree patch. When I went into the town I went on a little truck. I didn't go there for a month. I stayed at home. After a certain point one couldn't go into town any more, so I don't know who was there and what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know who Savovic is?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I knew him, but I don't know who he is or what he was and what his responsibility was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, please move closer to the microphone. Would the usher please assist him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you know of the police commander Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: No, just by hearing. I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, he was the chief; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that if would have taken hundreds of responsible people for the thousands of Muslims that died?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the Vasiljevic case, and maybe I'm just making a point, he indicated that he was embarrassed that he was here for Vasiljevic based on the fact that several thousand people had died and he was the only one being held responsible, and so I guess I was just making that point, Your Honour, but it is part of the earlier record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly. Certainly it would have taken -- I can't say several hundred, hundreds. Maybe just 20 or 50 people responsible, because a couple of could not have inflicted this much evil on that municipality and on the scattered villages, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions, Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: My name is Jens Dieckmann, and I'm Defence co-counsel for Mr. Sredoje Lukic, and I have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: As far as I have understood you correctly, you know Sredoje Lukic, and you know him as a policeman from Visegrad, an ordinary policeman of lower rank, and you know his parents as well. You know him also as a family man, as the father of two small children at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, that's so many questions. Just put them one --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sorry. It was just to sum it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: My question was if he knows he is married and has two small children at this time.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he was married, but as to how many children he had, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Sredoje Lukic was afraid of Milan Lukic; true?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Well, by worth of mouth, yes, he was. People said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could you give us the reasons why you think that he was afraid of Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: This was this gentleman Music Safet. We were sitting in cafe in Sarajevo and we were, you know, talking, and he told me that he had been detained up there in the Visegrad spa, in the Visegradska Banja, and that he came in a Volkswagen vehicle with another policeman, I guess his name was Niko, this policeman and there were more detainees there. And then this Safet, I said Safet, yes it was Safet, and then Sredoje went into the cellar of that room where a couple of people were detained, and he took out this Safet and his brother. The last name of both of them is Music. So he put them in his car and he took them home. That, in other words, was a humane gesture on his part. And as for what I started talking about, Muradif, this neighbour of mine, he also told him that he would not kill him, that he should be afraid but that he had to justify his actions to this other guy, and he said, "I'm just going to shoot some shots into the air and you go down there and go to your people in Zepa," and that's the way it actually happened. He told him, "Halt, halt," and then he shot a few shots in the air, and then he ran away and he panted, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. VG-47, on the 12th of August, 2008, you have had a meeting with two persons of the Prosecutor. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Could you kindly repeat the question? I wasn't actually listening. 12th of August and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: On the 12th of August, 2008, you have had a meeting with two persons of the Prosecutor. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And the reason of this meeting was to clarify your prior statements to the ICTY and in the Vasiljevic case; true?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And during this meeting you stated that you would like to make a few comments in defence of Sredoje Lukic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: This is exactly what I just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And this statement you made by your free will and your own motivation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes. I was glad that he acted in that way towards his next door neighbours, for had he taken him to Prelovo, he certainly would not have returned alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in this meeting you expressed your opinion that Sredoje Lukic should not be prosecuted, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: All I know is this: I don't know why Sredoje should have allowed himself for things to have come to this. If he had done something, he should be -- he should actually be held to account, if he is to blame for something.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. And, VG-47, from your personal experience with Sredoje Lukic, do you agree with me that he's a friendly person, a person of a good character and a good person? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I agree with you in respect of the period in which we knew each other up to the war. After that, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your testimony. We thank you for giving it. You may now leave. We are going to take a break. Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. I'll be handling this witness, Your Honour, but first I wanted to talk about the protective measures. It appears from looking at the transcript in the Vasiljevic case a colloquy between Judge Hunt and Mr. Groome that Judge Hunt said that I'm assured with private session there would be no sound and there is never any camera on the witness so that would probably be sufficient for you. And Mr. Groome said yes, Your Honour. And then Judge Hunt went on to say we can proceed and the witness can feel safe that he cannot be seen and he cannot be heard. I think he testified in private session is what I gather from this, but I believe that face distortion and facial -- and voice distortion would be sufficient for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll grant the facial and voice distortion. I understand it will take 15 minutes to set up whatever is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll adjourn and return in 15 minutes. --- Break taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May the usher show the witness a pseudonym sheet, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, I've asked the court usher to show you what's called a pseudonym sheet and ask is that your name next to the reference to VG-97?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And that your date of birth on that sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you -- can we correct the date of birth? Could you write in your correct date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And would you also sign that sheet, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders the pseudonym sheet as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P27 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, the Chamber has ordered certain protective measures with respect to your testimony as we discussed. You will have a voice and an image distortion so that persons cannot recognise your face or your voice. So I will be referring to you, and everyone will be referring to as either sir or VG-97. That is your pseudonym in this -- for your testimony. Sir, in the spring of 1992, in which municipality did you live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: In Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you live in a particular section of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes. In a place called Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, did you provide a statement to ICTY investigators in March of 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And when you gave this statement it was originally typed in English, and was it read back to you in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you then sign the English version of this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: I think that I signed both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, since coming to The Hague have you had an opportunity to review your statement in your Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like the statement to be brought up on the screen because there's a few corrections to be made, if possible. It was admitted -- it was allowed yesterday to be added to our exhibit list, so I don't have a 65 ter number. Would the ERN be sufficient? The English is 02021904 to 190 -- 1910, and the -- in the Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I'm a little bit confused. Do we have a 65 ter number for this statement and is it on the list of 65 ter? I'm a little bit confused, so that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was -- it was admitted orally by Your Honour yesterday. He's one of the witness as testifying this week whose 92 ter statement be added to the list in our previous motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Are they trying to find it? I think the court deputy is trying to find the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The ERN doesn't work? Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's there now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. May we go to page 3 in each of the English and the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, unfortunately the paragraphs are not numbered, but it is the third paragraph down from the top, and, sir, I asked you this question in proofing. The word in the English statement says "Revengers" and you said this is not the correct word. I'd like you to look at your statement in B/C/S and tell me if the word "Revengers "is there or if it's another word.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: The word is okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. The third paragraph down in the B/C/S, the second sentence refers to a word "Osvetnici." What is that word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not clear to me what you're trying to correct in relation to the word "Revengers." Is that the correct word?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, did you mean to say "Revengers" when you gave this statement? Revengers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll withdraw that correction. Could we go to page 4, please. Okay. The fourth paragraph down, the third line and the fourth line in the English there's the worth faith, f-a-i-t-h. Faith. Is that the word that you wanted to use in that sentence, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: I don't another where you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you look at the Bosnian version of your statement where it starts, "With many times during the month of June 1992 ..." Could you read that sentence to us, what the first half of that paragraph says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: "Often during June 1992, I would see Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic and Sredoje Lukic taking people away."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: The "The first time this was around the 15th of June when Milan Lukic with a red pass at took away Mujo Kurspahic and nobody knows to this day, I apologise, this was around the 15th of June when Milan Lukic took away you Mujo Kurspahic with his red Passat. No one knows to this day what happened to Mujo. The second time Milan Lukic took away Nedzad Ribac in Nedzad's car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's beyond what the Prosecutor wants.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to correct the English version of the statement on the record. You didn't refer in those statements anything having to do with faith, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: What faith are you referring to? I'm not clear on that? Whose faith?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I think we discussed this yesterday. In the English translation the word "faith" shows up and I asked you if that's what you said. Did you use the word "faith" when you gave the statement to the ICTY investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: You have to show me the exact part of the statement where this faith is referred to and I will immediately give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, it's only in the English version, sir, and I don't -- can you read English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: My question just -- forget about the statement. Did you ever mention -- discuss with the ICTY investigator anything to do with faith, as in such as religious faith or faith in something? Did you discuss that in this ICTY statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: I did discuss it when I was giving my personals to them. I said that my -- I was of the Muslim or Bosniak or Islamic faith.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. When you reviewed your statement in the Bosnian language is everything contained in this statement truthful and accurate to the best of your knowledge with regard to the events that you witnessed and experienced in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you the same questions that were put to you by the investigator in 2001, would your answers be the same as those that you provided in 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we ask that the statement be admitted in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P28 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution does not seek to admit his prior testimony in the Vasiljevic case and withdraws our motion to seek to admit that testimony, and I will just proceed with a short examination if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, in 1992 did you know a person by the name of Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how did you know him? Was it from school or other associations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Milan Lukic already as a boy when I went to school. Mr. Milan Lukic went to the Hamid Besirevic secondary school centre, and I attended primary school; but I went every day to the new hotel taking milk there because we catered to the hotels in Visegrad, and I would see him in the street with other lads from Zupa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: How often would you see him at this time in your life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Almost every day when I used to go to take that milk there. And I went downtown every day, so I wasn't really interested in counting how many times I would see him or saw him, but I do know him and I know that he socialised with a certain Slavko Vujinovic, who I knew very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, after the war started in 1992, did you see Mr. Lukic then as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Had any period of time passed between the time the war started and the time you had seen him in school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes. Some seven or eight years elapsed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: When you saw Milan Lukic in 1992 after the war started, did you recognise him as the same person you had seen earlier as you described in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And, sir, in 1992 did you know any other person by the name of Milan Lukic or anyone who called himself Milan Lukic other than this person you've identified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: I did not know any other person by the name of Milan Lukic, nor was there any other person with the name of Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, in 1992 did you also known a person by the name of Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes, I did know Mr. Sredoje Lukic. I knew him for at least ten years, because the gentleman worked at the police station in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how often would you see Sredoje Lukic before the war started in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Well, I always saw him in town. He would be there. He would be present in the town of Visegrad, and he drove a red Moskvitch Aleko, a Russian-make vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like you to look around the courtroom very carefully and then tell us whether you recognise anyone in this courtroom other than myself and, if so, whom do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes, I do. To my left-hand side on the right-hand side is Mr. Sredoje Lukic. To the right-hand side of Sredoje Lukic is Mr. Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May the record reflect, Your Honour, that this witness has identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, as you heard a few moments ago your statement has been admitted into evidence so I'm not going to ask you many very detailed questions since the Judges have your statement and they have read it, and they can read everything that you have to say but I'm going to ask you a couple of questions about the events that happened in 1992. Did you ever see Milan Lukic driving a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I often saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And could you please describe the vehicle which -- in which he was driving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Lukic drove a red Passat and Zastava van which was also red.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how often would you see him driving the red Passat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Quite often. He frequently passed through Kosovo Polje in the direction of Sase from Visegrad or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you lived in the village of Kosovo Polje. Was this on the direct route between Sase and Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The road actually divides the settlement of Kosovo Polje. On the right-hand side there are the Orthodox Serbs, and on the left side of the road are the Bosniak Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And does this road lead to any other -- any other places that you mentioned in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: The road leads towards Zupa, and in Sase there is a right-hand turn towards Visegradska Banja, the Visegrad spa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see anyone else driving the red Passat? And I'm talking about driving, not being a passenger.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: In the course of 1992 or before 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: I saw nobody else drive that Passat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you see other passengers in the vehicle with Milan Lukic when he was driving the red Passat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Frequently there would be -- there would be two or three men, and sometimes the gentleman went on his own or with just one co-passenger in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Would you see Sredoje Lukic riding in the car with Milan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you describe witnessing a number of crimes committed by Milan and Sredoje Lukic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber on approximately how many occasions you witnessed crimes being committed by one or both of these gentlemen where the red Passat was present at the scene of the crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: On at least three occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a man by the name of Stanko Pecikoza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Mr. Stanko Pecikoza very well. He was very hospitable and he had his private sawmill. He often helped us at Kosovo Polje during the war. On one occasion after incidents had become more frequent and we couldn't hide out there any longer, my father had asked Stanko Pecikoza to take me up with him at the sawmill for me to be safer, because up there they didn't touch anyone, although the workers at the sawmill were Muslims, whereas down -- down there people would be attacked, and Stanko agreed. On the 10th of June, with two neighbours I went to Stanko Pecikoza's sawmill to help myself and help out with the work there too. And we were about a dozen, Serbs and Muslims alike. And at that moment I heard Stanko's wife crying out in mourning. From the direction of the road towards the sawmill we heard a siren, and the woman cried out and -- saying, "Alas, there comes Micko." And when we all -- nobody said a word, and Mr. Lukic drove up in his red Passat. A soldier stepped out from the Passat. He was providing security for Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic never got out of the car. He opened the door and greeted everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. May I stop you? Sorry. When you say "Micko," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: I mean Milan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, did Milan Lukic say anything to you at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is Milan also called Micko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard -- sorry. Your Honours, I heard the lady saying these words.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm not sure which lady --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which lady? What lady?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I spoke about the events, I said that Stanko's wife cried out and said, "Alas, there comes Micko."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And who is Micko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you know what the ethnicity of Mr. Pecikoza was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Mr. Pecikoza was a Serb of Orthodox nationality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I believe I'll go back to my previous question whether Milan Lukic said anything to you when he was in the car and he pulled up to Stanko Pecikoza's house at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes. He said the following words: He first said "pomoz bog, braco Srbi," which means God may help you fellow Serbs, and "merhaba," Turks, and then he said, "Mr. Stanko, do these Turks obey you?" Upon which Stanko replied, "Mind your own business," and that there was no need for him to come to his yard and that all these people were decent, honourable people who had done no harm to anyone. Mr. Lukic replied, "Yes, they're good. They're all right, but they will go to Bajina Basta nonetheless," by which he meant he would -- that he would throw us all into the lake and that we would end up at Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And where is Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Bajina Basta is downstream from Visegrad, and there's also a hydro power plant on the Drina River by the same name some 40 kilometres from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is that the end of the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: No. That is the spot where a hydro power plant dam was made on the Drina River which created an artificial lake of Bajina Basta where -- where our bodies would end up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know where Mr. Pecikoza is today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Mr. Pecikoza is not alive anymore. Unfortunately he was killed on the 19th of June, 1992. I don't know who killed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we recessing at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: To not breaking continuity, Your Honour, would you object to taking a recess and just beginning fresh tomorrow? I can only ask a few questions in five minutes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ask them. Ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. 97, in 1992 how old were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: I was 21 and a half years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you stated on direct examination that you were three years younger than Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you were in primary school he was in secondary school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you never played with him directly as a child?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that as a young boy Milan Lukic had Muslim friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: He would have had to have Muslim friends just the same as I had Serbian -- Serb friends, because it was a mixed surrounding, a mixed environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in your statement of 2001, was that the first time you'd ever given an official statement in an investigation related to the tragedy in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes, to an international tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is that to say that you'd given other statements before that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: To whom have you given statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: When we crossed the Drina and came to the left bank in June 1992. There were people there who asked us about what had happened, and a teacher by the name of Sabit Hota [phoen] had some kind of register of events, and he put down our statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you gave statements as to the alleged crimes in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: I gave statements about what I had experienced at Kosovo Polje from April to the 19th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you remained in the area until mid-July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: I spent part of the time at the village of Hamzici until mid-July 1992, because due to the heavy shelling the houses we lived in were badly damaged and we were exposed to artillery and tank fire. So we had to withdraw to another village, Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in your statement of 2001 you indicated that early on you saw Dragan Tomic in a jeep near Stanko Pecikoza's home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you indicated in your statement that you did not dare stop them. Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: They were armed, and they were moving toward Homar where the command of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian community was. I didn't dare stop them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Tomic was the commander of the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he was commander, but I'm sure that he was in a high-ranking position in the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know who Perisic was as chief of police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was your -- what was your understanding of Perisic's role in the community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-97
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Risto Perisic as the teacher who taught me Serbo-Croatian at the secondary school centre. When I -- at the time when I went to school, he was active in the volleyball club by the name of Drina. He played a major role in the organisation of the SDS and the establishment of the Serbian municipality of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, we have to stop there for today. We'll resume tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of August, 2008, at 8.50 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.
